paragraphs: Large network models can contain recurring patterns whose associated parameters are similar. Learning these parameters in groups can make estimation more efficient, but the useful groups may not be known beforehand. This paper develops a Bayesian approach that infers the grouping while learning an undirected graphical model, rather than requiring a separate, predetermined assignment of parameters to groups.

The method places a Dirichlet process prior on the parameters to represent their unknown grouping. Computing the resulting posterior involves intractable quantities, so the authors introduce two approximate inference algorithms. One uses Metropolis-Hastings sampling with auxiliary variables; the other uses Gibbs sampling with a stripped Beta approximation, called Gibbs SBA.

In simulations, both algorithms outperform conventional maximum likelihood estimation. Gibbs SBA also performs close to Gibbs sampling that calculates the likelihood exactly. On Senate voting data, models learned with Gibbs SBA generalize better than those learned by maximum likelihood. These findings support learning shared parameter structure alongside the model, while using approximation to make the Bayesian computation feasible.
neurips-2013-bayesian-estimation-of-late.tldr: A Bayesian method discovers parameter groups in undirected graphical models and improves estimation over maximum likelihood in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: A sensory neuron's receptive field describes how it combines input across space and time. Estimating this description can require many coefficients, creating statistical and computational difficulties when recordings are limited. The paper represents a receptive field as a sum of several simpler filters, each separating its spatial and temporal components. This low-rank representation remains accurate for strongly oriented receptive fields in the examples considered.

The authors develop Bayesian reduced rank regression with a prior obtained by restricting a matrix normal distribution to low-rank matrices. Additional covariance priors encourage sparse, smooth, localized spatial and temporal components. They provide two inference routes: a fully Bayesian blocked-Gibbs sampler and a faster approximate method based on alternating optimization of conditional marginal likelihood.

The methods accommodate Gaussian and Poisson noise models. In the examples studied, the representation reduces parameter counts from thousands or tens of thousands to hundreds. Evaluations on retina and V1 recordings show substantially better accuracy and speed than full-rank estimation, demonstrating the statistical and computational value of the compact representation in these settings.
neurips-2013-bayesian-inference-for-low-.tldr: Bayesian low-rank receptive-field models substantially improve estimation accuracy and speed on the reported retina and V1 data.

paragraphs: Text can be represented using many possible word sequences, but the resulting feature space can be enormous. This paper learns a compact collection of word k-grams without labels by asking which dictionary best compresses the documents. Its minimum description length objective chooses features that minimize the cost of reconstructing the text without losing information.

Document compression is formulated as a binary optimization problem. The authors solve it approximately through a sequence of reweighted linear programs, which are efficient to solve and can be parallelized. Because feature selection is unsupervised, the resulting dictionary can be extracted once and reused across different analysis and prediction tasks.

The reported compressed representation is two orders of magnitude smaller than the full k-gram feature space while matching its text categorization accuracy. The authors also demonstrate exploratory analysis with these features. The smaller representation speeds training, and it can make structure easier to see in unsupervised tasks and reduce the labeled training data needed for supervised learning.
neurips-2013-compressive-feature-learnin.tldr: Learning text features through lossless compression yields a much smaller representation that matches full-feature categorization accuracy in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Seriation reconstructs a linear ordering of variables from similarity information whose original order is unknown. The paper studies this problem through optimization over permutations, connecting it to applications such as archaeological ordering and shotgun gene sequencing. The central challenge is to turn pairwise similarity information into a coherent sequence, including when that information contains noise.

The authors prove that seriation is equivalent to the quadratic 2-sum permutation problem for a particular class of similarity matrices. This qualification matters: the stated equivalence concerns that class. Starting from a problem that admits an exact spectral solution in the noiseless setting, they construct a convex relaxation of 2-sum to improve robustness when similarities are noisy.

The relaxation also accommodates additional structural constraints on the ordering. This makes it useful for semi-supervised seriation, where some information about the desired solution is available alongside similarities. Numerical experiments cover archaeological data, Markov chains, and gene sequences, examining the approach across different sources of ordering information.
neurips-2013-convex-relaxations-for-perm.tldr: A convex relaxation connects seriation to permutation optimization and supports noisy similarities and additional ordering constraints.

paragraphs: Decision trees can grow exponentially in node count as their depth increases, making memory a barrier to richer classifiers. This is particularly relevant for mobile and embedded processors. The paper proposes decision jungles: ensembles of rooted directed acyclic graphs that allow multiple paths to reach the same leaf, sharing nodes within the classifier.

Training must determine both which features to use and how the graph should connect. The authors introduce and compare two node-merging algorithms that optimize these choices jointly. Node splitting and merging use the same training objective, the weighted sum of leaf entropies, so expansion and compression are guided by a common measure of classification quality.

Across the evaluated datasets, decision jungles use dramatically less memory and considerably improve generalization compared with decision forests and several other baselines. The findings show that shared graph structure can support both compact storage and strong classification performance. The contribution therefore addresses the memory cost of deeper decision models while also improving predictive behavior in the reported experiments.
neurips-2013-decision-jungles-compact-an.tldr: Decision jungles share nodes within decision graphs, reducing memory use and improving generalization in the reported classification experiments.

paragraphs: The paper studies binary Bayesian networks with two layers, where every variable in the upper layer is hidden. Learning such noisy-or models means discovering the hidden variables, their connections to observed variables, and the associated parameters. The authors provide a polynomial-time learning algorithm with provable guarantees for a structurally defined family of these networks.

The key condition is quartet learnability: each hidden variable has four children that share no other parents. Such a quartet uniquely identifies its hidden parent and allows the parameters involving that parent to be learned. The algorithm combines a quartet test for detecting this shared-parent pattern with a conditional mutual information test for parameter estimation.

Already learned hidden variables can also be subtracted from the model, revealing new qualifying quartets and substantially enlarging the class of learnable structures. The authors prove polynomial sample complexity and compare the method experimentally with variational EM. Its guarantees depend on the stated structural conditions, making the quartet pattern central to both identifiability and efficient learning.
neurips-2013-discovering-hidden-variable.tldr: Quartet-based tests enable provably efficient recovery of hidden variables and parameters in a structured family of noisy-or networks.

paragraphs: Sampling from a probability distribution over many discrete variables can be difficult, including when a graphical model specifies the distribution. The paper introduces PAWS, an algorithm that approaches sampling through transformations of the discrete search space and combinatorial search. Its design allows existing fast combinatorial optimization tools to serve as black-box components.

PAWS first embeds the original set in a higher-dimensional space. It then uses universal hash functions to project randomly into a lower-dimensional subspace, which combinatorial search methods explore. This embed-and-project construction provides a sampling guarantee: the resulting distribution is within an arbitrarily small constant factor of the target probabilities.

The authors demonstrate efficient sampling on strongly interacting Ising grids and software verification instances using state-of-the-art search tools. In those reported cases, MCMC and variational methods fail. The results connect a formal approximation guarantee with practical use of combinatorial solvers, showing that tools developed for discrete search can also support difficult probabilistic sampling tasks.
neurips-2013-embed-and-project-discrete-.tldr: PAWS combines universal hashing with combinatorial search to sample discrete distributions with a multiplicative approximation guarantee.

paragraphs: This paper targets ridge regression when there are far more features than observations. In this regime, the standard dual-space approach has running time O(n²p), where n counts observations and p counts features. The authors develop SRHT-DRR to reduce this computational cost while also analyzing the statistical risk of the resulting procedure.

The algorithm preconditions the design matrix with a randomized Walsh-Hadamard transform and then subsamples features. The transformation and feature reduction together yield a stated running time of O(np log(n)). Relative to the standard expression, the dependence multiplying np changes from n to log(n), which is the central computational improvement claimed for the targeted high-dimensional setting.

The paper provides risk bounds under a fixed-design formulation and presents experiments using synthetic and real datasets. These components address complementary questions: how the method's estimation risk can be controlled and how it behaves on data. The contribution combines a faster computational route with statistical analysis specifically for ridge regression in the many-features, fewer-observations regime.
neurips-2013-faster-ridge-regression-via.tldr: SRHT-DRR accelerates ridge regression with many more features than observations using a randomized transform and feature subsampling.

paragraphs: Repeated decisions under uncertainty require balancing the value of trying alternatives against using what already appears rewarding. This paper studies how people manage that balance in a multi-armed bandit task. The authors compare human choices with models that differ in how they represent uncertainty and how much computation they use to select actions.

The best account of subjects' trial-by-trial choices combines a forgetful Bayesian learning model with Knowledge Gradient, a partially myopic decision policy. This combination fits choices better than the compared alternatives, including optimal Bayesian learning and risk minimization, epsilon-greedy, and win-stay-lose-shift. The finding concerns the observed behavior in the studied task.

The model also comes closest to optimal Bayesian performance among the compared heuristics with the same computational complexity. Those heuristics are all substantially less complex than the optimal model. Together, the behavioral fit and performance comparison suggest that limited-memory learning paired with partially short-sighted planning can help explain effective human exploration without requiring the full computation of optimal Bayesian decision-making.
neurips-2013-forgetful-bayes-and-myopic-.tldr: A forgetful Bayesian learner with Knowledge Gradient best explains the reported human bandit choices among the models compared.

paragraphs: Financial time-series analysis often depends on estimating how multiple variables move together. Copula functions provide a way to express these dependencies, but treating the copula as constant can be inaccurate when other variables influence the relationship. This paper develops a Bayesian framework for conditional copulas that allows dependence to change with the information being conditioned on.

The framework relates copula parameters nonlinearly to conditioning variables. This makes the dependence model responsive to covariates, rather than fixing one relationship across all observations. The central modeling choice is therefore to estimate how dependencies vary with context, with the paper's Gaussian process formulation providing the conditional approach identified in its title.

The authors evaluate predictions of time-varying dependencies for several equities and currencies. They report consistent performance gains over static copulas and other time-varying copula methods in those evaluations. The findings support modeling nonlinear relationships between conditioning information and dependence parameters when analyzing these financial series, where a constant dependence description may miss relevant variation.
neurips-2013-gaussian-process-conditiona.tldr: Bayesian conditional copulas model covariate-dependent relationships and improve dependency predictions in the reported equity and currency evaluations.

paragraphs: Finding the most probable configuration of an undirected graphical model can be expressed as an energy minimization problem. Combinatorial solvers can return provably optimal discrete solutions, but large problems often exceed their practical reach. Convex relaxations can handle large sparse graphs and often produce good approximations, creating an opportunity to combine the two approaches.

The paper uses information from a solved convex relaxation to shrink the portion of the graphical model that needs combinatorial search. The exact solver is then applied to only a small fraction of the original problem. This reduction is designed to retain a global solution of the original discrete problem while limiting the expensive search.

The authors demonstrate the method on a computer vision energy minimization benchmark. Its significance lies in using a tractable relaxation to guide exact optimization: the approximate formulation helps determine where combinatorial effort is needed. The reported approach thereby enables optimal solutions for large problems through coordination between convex and combinatorial techniques.
neurips-2013-global-map-optimality-by-sh.tldr: Convex relaxation narrows the region requiring combinatorial search, enabling globally optimal solutions to large graphical-model problems.

paragraphs: Low-rank subspace clustering represents data through a union of low-dimensional subspaces. Its variational Bayesian formulation has shown good performance, but optimization can get trapped in local minima. This paper develops an exact global solver for that formulation, together with a more computationally efficient approximation, addressing a specific obstacle to Bayesian learning in this model.

The authors first prove that the variational Bayesian model contains substantial redundancy. Exploiting this property separates the optimization into small subproblems with few unknowns. Each subproblem's stationary conditions can be expressed as polynomial equations, allowing the exact solver to use a homotopy method to solve them.

For greater efficiency, the approximate variant reduces its stationary condition to a polynomial equation in a single variable. Experiments show the usefulness of the approach. The key contribution is the model-specific mathematical reduction: redundancy that might appear to complicate learning instead enables a global solution strategy. The exactness applies to the variational Bayesian optimization problem, whose formulation is itself an approximation to full Bayesian inference.
neurips-2013-global-solver-and-its-effic.tldr: Model redundancy enables an exact global solver and an efficient approximate solver for variational Bayesian low-rank subspace clustering.

paragraphs: The paper estimates the ratio q/p, where p is a probability density and q may be another density or a more general function. Such ratios are useful when averaging under one distribution using samples from another, as in importance sampling. They also arise in covariate shift, where training and target distributions differ.

The authors reformulate ratio estimation as a kernel-based inverse problem, expressed through a Fredholm integral equation of the first kind. Combining this formulation with regularization produces the FIRE family of estimators. This gives a shared mathematical basis for constructing algorithms and studying their behavior, rather than treating ratio estimation only as an isolated fitting task.

Theoretical results include concentration bounds and convergence rates for Gaussian kernels on Euclidean spaces and smooth submanifolds. When samples from both distributions are available, the authors also introduce Cross-Density Cross-Validation for fully unsupervised parameter selection. Experiments, including classification under covariate shift, provide encouraging results. Together, these contributions connect estimation, theoretical analysis, and parameter choice within one framework.
neurips-2013-inverse-density-as-an-inver.tldr: FIRE treats density-ratio estimation as a regularized kernel inverse problem, with theory and unsupervised parameter selection.

paragraphs: Recovering a low-rank matrix from noisy observations can benefit from knowing more than its rank. This paper uses a Bayesian formulation to incorporate additional structure, such as sparsity, into reconstruction. The aim is to make the assumed properties of the underlying matrix part of inference, allowing information beyond low-rankedness to guide the recovered result.

The authors derive an efficient approximate message passing algorithm from belief propagation to carry out this Bayesian inference. The algorithm provides a computational procedure for reconstructing matrices under the structural model. Its role is to make use of the richer formulation while keeping the inference process efficient.

The same approach is applied to clustering by expressing clustering as low-rank matrix reconstruction with an additional structural property. Numerical experiments show that the proposed method outperforms Lloyd's K-means algorithm. This result supports the usefulness of the reconstruction perspective for the tested clustering problems: cluster discovery can be approached through structured matrix estimation using the same inference machinery.
neurips-2013-low-rank-matrix-reconstruct.tldr: Bayesian approximate message passing exploits matrix structure for reconstruction and outperforms Lloyd's K-means in the reported clustering experiments.

paragraphs: Connections in social networks reflect both similarities between people and the tendency to connect to popular individuals. This paper combines these influences within a mixed-membership stochastic blockmodel. The resulting probabilistic model includes node popularity alongside overlapping community membership, giving it a way to represent two distinct sources of network connectivity.

To learn the model at scale, the authors develop a nonconjugate variant of stochastic variational inference. They evaluate link prediction on eight real networks containing up to 60,000 nodes and on 24 benchmark networks. These tests examine whether the richer model improves predictions of connections while supporting networks of substantial size.

The method predicts links better than the mixed-membership stochastic blockmodel in the reported evaluations. Benchmark results also show that popularity is essential to high accuracy in the studied settings with skewed degree distributions and noisy links. This identifies a concrete reason to model popularity explicitly: community membership alone may not adequately explain connectivity when some nodes have many more links than others.
neurips-2013-modeling-overlapping-commun.tldr: Adding node popularity to overlapping-community models improves link prediction, especially in the reported noisy networks with skewed degrees.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents need to explore actions whose consequences remain uncertain. This paper studies posterior sampling as an alternative to encouraging exploration through optimistic estimates. The algorithm operates in episodes of known duration and represents uncertainty through a probability distribution over possible Markov decision processes, naturally allowing prior knowledge to enter learning.

At the start of each episode, the agent updates its distribution using the available information and samples one possible decision process. It then follows the policy that would be optimal for that sampled process throughout the episode. This provides a conceptually simple exploration mechanism driven by uncertainty about the environment.

The authors establish an expected-regret bound of approximately τS√(AT), with logarithmic factors suppressed, where τ is episode length, S and A count states and actions, and T is elapsed time. The bound is close to the stated state of the art and among the first for an approach without optimism. Simulations show substantial improvements over existing algorithms with similar regret guarantees.
neurips-2013-more-efficient-reinforcemen.tldr: Posterior sampling provides simple episodic exploration with a strong expected-regret bound and favorable simulation results.

paragraphs: Camera shake can blur different image regions by different amounts, especially when rotation produces greater blur farther from an unknown center. Recovering a sharp image therefore requires estimating a spatially varying blur operator. This paper develops a blind deblurring algorithm using ideas from Bayesian inference and convex analysis to handle that non-uniformity.

Its objective includes a spatially adaptive penalty coupling the unknown sharp image, blur operator, and noise level. As these estimates change, the penalty adjusts to local blur and image structure. Regions with severe blur or few prominent edges receive less influence, allowing regions with moderate blur and informative edges to guide estimation.

This automatic adjustment performs the selection of useful image evidence without explicit structure-selection heuristics. The authors describe an optimization strategy that is simpler than existing methods and virtually free of parameters requiring adjustment. Theoretical analysis and experiments on real images support the method, connecting its adaptive weighting mechanism to the practical challenge of recovering images affected by uneven camera shake.
neurips-2013-non-uniform-camera-shake-re.tldr: A spatially adaptive penalty guides non-uniform camera deblurring toward image regions with more informative edges and less severe blur.

paragraphs: This paper studies online decision-making in finite episodic Markov decision processes whose loss function may change between episodes. Performance is measured by regret against the best stationary policy: the learner should accumulate little additional loss relative to that fixed-policy benchmark. The setting therefore combines sequential decisions within episodes with changing losses across episodes.

The authors assume a finite action set and a state space arranged into L layers, with transitions permitted only between consecutive layers. They analyze a variant of Relative Entropy Policy Search under both bandit feedback and full information. Writing X and A for the numbers of states and actions, the respective regret bounds are 2√(LXAT log(XA/L)) and 2L√(T log(XA/L)).

Both bounds grow with the square root of the number of episodes T, so the guaranteed regret per episode decreases as more episodes are played. The authors state that these guarantees substantially improve earlier results under milder assumptions and cannot be significantly improved under general assumptions. The layered transition structure remains an explicit condition of the analysis.
neurips-2013-online-learning-in-episodic.tldr: A Relative Entropy Policy Search variant achieves strong regret guarantees for layered episodic decision processes with changing losses.

paragraphs: The paper studies a social network whose members repeatedly estimate a changing state of the world. Each person receives a private signal and communicates with neighbors at every time step. The underlying state follows a geometric random walk, so learning requires continual tracking rather than convergence toward one fixed unknown value.

The authors formulate tracking as optimization of a global loss and derive two update mechanisms from different decompositions of that objective. They establish a tight bound on how quickly the state can change while individuals still track it with bounded variance. They also derive explicit expressions for each person's steady-state mean-square deviation from the true state.

Only one of the two estimators achieves the optimal mean-square deviation. This shows that how the global objective is decomposed affects the quality of distributed learning, even when both mechanisms address the same tracking problem. The paper additionally bounds finite-time regret measured through average estimation errors, complementing its steady-state analysis with a guarantee over a finite observation period.
neurips-2013-online-learning-of-dynamic-.tldr: Two distributed tracking rules reveal how objective decomposition affects accuracy when social-network agents learn a dynamically changing state.

paragraphs: Low-rank matrix completion fills in missing matrix entries while favoring a compact underlying structure. This paper introduces a class of algorithms built around penalties on the matrix's singular values. These penalties control the spectral representation of the completed matrix, making the treatment of singular values central to how low rank is encouraged.

The authors express the penalty through a mixture model and introduce suitable latent variables. This probabilistic construction yields an Expectation-Maximization algorithm for obtaining a maximum a posteriori estimate of the completed matrix. The resulting procedure repeatedly applies soft thresholding, adapting the shrinkage coefficients associated with the singular values as optimization proceeds.

The adaptive coefficients allow the regularization applied to the singular values to evolve during estimation. The authors describe the algorithm as simple to implement and scalable to large matrices. Numerical comparisons with recent alternatives support the usefulness of the approach for matrix completion. The contribution links a probabilistic penalty representation to a practical iterative algorithm with adaptive spectral regularization.
neurips-2013-probabilistic-low-rank-matr.tldr: A probabilistic matrix-completion method adaptively shrinks singular values through an Expectation-Maximization algorithm.

paragraphs: Inference in general Ising models faces two computational obstacles. High treewidth can make tree-based methods intractable, while strong interactions can cause Gibbs sampling to require exponential time to reach its stationary distribution. With a limited sampling budget, using the original model can therefore leave the sampler far from the behavior it is meant to represent.

The paper proposes projecting the model's parameters onto a set for which fast mixing is guaranteed. It develops this projection under several divergence measures, providing different ways to express the discrepancy between the original and modified models. The resulting parameters change the model while placing it in a regime where sampling converges quickly.

The authors find that Gibbs sampling with projected parameters is more accurate than sampling with the original parameters when interactions are strong and sampling time is limited. The finding highlights a practical tradeoff: altering parameters can improve finite-time inference when convergence is otherwise too slow. The reported advantage is tied to those interaction strengths and time constraints.
neurips-2013-projecting-ising-model-para.tldr: Projecting Ising parameters into a fast-mixing set improves reported sampling accuracy under strong interactions and limited computation time.

paragraphs: Submodular functions appear in learning, signal processing, and computer vision, but minimizing them can be computationally challenging. This paper develops an approach that exploits existing decomposability in the function being optimized. Its aim is an exact, practical procedure that is easy to implement and parallelize without cumbersome parameter tuning.

The central step reformulates discrete submodular minimization as a continuous best approximation problem. A sequence of reflections solves this continuous formulation. Its solution can then be automatically thresholded to produce an optimal discrete solution, linking continuous computation directly to the original discrete optimization task.

Because the method solves both formulations, it has applications in learning, inference, and reconstruction. Experiments on two image segmentation tasks demonstrate benefits of the proposed algorithms. The important structural condition is the decomposability the method exploits: the contribution uses that available organization to obtain a practical optimization route. The automatic thresholding also makes the continuous solution useful without giving up optimality in the discrete problem.
neurips-2013-reflection-methods-for-user.tldr: Reflection-based optimization exploits decomposability to solve submodular minimization exactly through a continuous formulation and automatic thresholding.

paragraphs: Ensemble training can face a memory constraint that prevents retaining all available examples. This paper introduces a reservoir that stores a limited number of samples for learning. The approach occupies a middle ground between offline and online training: the learner keeps a restricted collection of examples available for use while operating within a bounded storage budget.

The authors examine basic strategies for filling the reservoir and introduce Greedy Edge Expectation Maximization, or GEEM, for boosting. GEEM maintains reservoir contents by viewing examples through their projections into the response space of weak classifiers. This makes the classifiers' responses to examples central to the selection of what remains stored.

An efficient implementation makes the approach tractable in practice. Experiments on several computer vision datasets show that it outperforms both online and offline methods in a memory-constrained setting. The findings support reservoir management as an important part of ensemble learning when storage is limited, with the reported advantage specifically established under that resource constraint.
neurips-2013-reservoir-boosting-between-.tldr: GEEM manages a limited training reservoir for boosting and outperforms compared online and offline methods under memory constraints.

paragraphs: The paper proposes calcium imaging through randomized spatial projections at each time step, rather than measurements at individual locations. It develops scalable nonnegative deconvolution methods to recover neuronal spike sequences from these compressed observations. Rank-penalized matrix factorization also addresses demixing the neurons' spatial locations.

By exploiting sparse spiking, the authors demonstrate that measurements per time step can be significantly fewer than the number of neurons. This could enable faster imaging of larger populations compared with raster scanning. The problem has distinctive structure: its sensing matrix is block diagonal, and its non-orthogonal sparse basis extends across multiple time steps.

The authors analyze these features in a noiseless setting using connections between compressed sensing and conic geometry. For certain classes of spiking processes, they obtain tight approximations to the measurement count needed for perfect deconvolution and identify a phase transition. The required rate depends on properties of the spiking process beyond average sparsity, showing that mean activity alone does not determine the recovery threshold.
neurips-2013-sparse-nonnegative-deconvol.tldr: Compressed calcium measurements can recover sparse neural activity, with noiseless recovery thresholds depending on more than average spiking sparsity.

paragraphs: This paper approaches principal component analysis, or PCA, as a stochastic optimization problem. The central contribution is an algorithmic treatment of that formulation: the authors propose a new stochastic approximation method called Matrix Stochastic Gradient, abbreviated MSG. Their focus is on how PCA can be solved through this optimization perspective.

Alongside MSG, the paper introduces Capped MSG as a practical variant. The contribution therefore includes both the proposed stochastic approximation algorithm and a version explicitly intended for practical use. These are presented as methods for the same PCA problem, with Capped MSG forming part of the paper's effort to connect the optimization formulation to an implementable procedure.

The authors study the method theoretically and empirically. The work thus combines mathematical investigation with experimental examination of the proposed approach. Its stated contribution is the formulation and study of MSG and its practical variant; the supplied abstract reports no particular comparative outcome. The supported takeaway is a new stochastic optimization route for PCA, investigated through both analysis and experiments.
neurips-2013-stochastic-optimization-of-.tldr: The paper introduces Matrix Stochastic Gradient and its practical Capped MSG variant for PCA, studying the approach theoretically and empirically.
